newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Algerian voters united in desire for peace.
newsitem.headline: Algerian voters united in desire for peace.

text.p: Algerians voting for different candidates from radically different parties in their general election on Thursday all seemed to be seeking one thing: Peace.

"I voted for peace" was the phrase most used by voters who cast ballots in the first parliamentary election since the nation of 29 million people plunged into violence and bloodshed more than five years ago.

Almost all voters -- old or young, men or women -- interviewed by Reuters in Algiers or appearing on state television and radio from across the vast country, spoke of peace at least once in answering questions why they had voted or whom they supported.
"I voted for peace, calm, democracy and freedom of speech," Hakim Gheli, a 27-year-old industrialist told Reuters.
"I voted for my children to live in peace," Saigi Akli, 78, said. "I voted for peace for me and my children," said Ahmed Yanagueni who cast the first ballot at an Algiers polling stations

It was the same in the sunlit streets of Algiers. Snatches of conversation caught from shoppers and people in pavement cafes showed the main topic in the whole election was how to return peace and stability to Algeria.
An estimated 60,000 people have died since violence started after the military-backed authorities in January 1992 cancelled Algeria's first multi-party general election.
The radical Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) had swept the first round in December 1991 and needed only 28 more seats for an absolute majority in parliament.
Since then, the FIS has been outlawed, and bombs, ambushes and assassinations have become a weary, frightening way of life.

Some of the most horrific killings have taken place since late last year. Hundreds of villagers, including women and children, have been massacred -- many by having their throats slit -- in attacks blamed on Moslem rebels.
Just a few days before the election two bombs ripped through buses and one blew up a market in Algiers killing at least 22 people and wounding about 120.
On Thursday, voters were putting their faith in the search for peace on independents, pro-government candidates, moderate Islamists, or anti-Islamists.
Not every eligible voter was participating. The outlawed FIS in Europe has called for a boycott and at least one fundamentalist near an Algiers polling station was heeding the call.
"I am not going to vote because I don't want to go back on my religious and political principles," he said.

He was well in the minority. By 11 a.m. (1000 GMT) nearly three million people had already voted, while the surge to the polls traditionally comes in the afternoon, at least in Algiers -- home to an estimated three to four million people.
